system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube dependence was admitted to the medicine service for weeks of intermittent post-prandial confusion and concern for hypoglycemia and malabsorption. Initial evaluation showed normal CBC, chemistries, and liver tests with low/normal ammonia; endocrinology supervised an overnight fast with tube feeds held, during which she did not become hypoglycemic, and fasting insulin/C-peptide/beta-hydroxybutyrate were within normal limits with proinsulin pending. Hepatology felt her episodes were not due to hepatic encephalopathy or cirrhosis; after a monitored high-protein meal she developed transient slurred speech and tremor with subsequent amnesia and post-meal rises in transaminases/albumin, raising concern for a possible urea cycle/metabolic contribution, and a urea cycle panel was sent (pending). EEG and brain MRI were normal. She was discharged home ambulatory with instructions to continue continuous tube feeds (transitioning to NutriHep when available), avoid oral caloric intake except water, continue rifaximin, hold atenolol given bradycardia, and follow up outpatient to review pending results and ongoing management of post-gastric surgery symptoms and hypoglycemia.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman s/p RNY with G-tube placement, p/w 1 week with

TECHNIQUE:  FRONTAL SUPINE AND UPRIGHT ABDOMINAL RADIOGRAPHS

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior abdominal radiographs, most recent on ___

of bowel in the right and left upper quadrant of are felt to represent colon. 
The urinary bladder is severely distended. The PEG tube is in appropriate
position. Surgical material in the epigastrium is from prior surgery.

Non specific bowel gas pattern. Severely distended urinary bladder. Correlate

EXAMINATION:  MRCP (MR ABD ___

INDICATION:  ___ hx of RNY gastric bypass in ___ complicated by frequent

small bowel intestinal overgrowth with multiple admissions for abdominal pain
p/w 1 week nausea with frequent episodes of dry heaving, diarrhea and 1 day of
constant mild epigastric pain. Treating for possible pancreatitis but concern
for biliary or ulcerative disease. Likely complicated by her complex GI
history.  // eval biliary anatomy

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1 and T2 weighted MR images of the abdomen were
obtained on a 1.5 Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging prior to, during,
and after the administration of 8 mL Gadavist gadolinium based contrast.  1 mL
Gadavist mixed with 50 mL water was also administered for oral contrast
through gastrostomy tube.

COMPARISON:  Ultrasound from ___ and CT from ___.

Mild linear atelectasis are seen in the lung bases, more on the left. There is
no pleural pericardial effusion.

The liver is normal in size and morphology. The signal characteristics of the
liver parenchyma are normal on T1 and T2WI. No focal liver lesions are seen.
Conventional arterial hepatic anatomy is demonstrated. The portal and hepatic
veins are patent.
The gallbladder is normal. The intra and extrahepatic biliary ducts are normal
in caliber.
The pancreas is normal in size and signal, without focal mass or ductal

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the medicine team. I understand you came in with nausea, dry heaving, diarrhea, and now constant epigastric pain. Can you tell me what’s bothering you most right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain. It’s right in the middle, like my old ulcer pain. And I can’t stop gagging even when there’s nothing to throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Is it different from the chronic pain you get around the G-tube site on the left?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The tube site always aches, but this is deeper and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the diarrhea? Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fever. The diarrhea is actually slowing down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER your labs were mostly reassuring—white count normal, liver tests normal. Your lipase was elevated, which can suggest pancreatitis, and your potassium was high at first but came down. They started IV fluids and pain and nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it pancreatitis again? Or is it another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we’re keeping both on the table. With your Roux-en-Y anatomy and history of marginal ulcers, ulcer disease is definitely possible. The lipase elevation could be mild pancreatitis, but we also want to make sure there isn’t a biliary issue or something else driving the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s an obstruction. I’ve had so many surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very reasonable worry. The abdominal x-ray didn’t show free air, and surgery has already evaluated you and doesn’t think this looks like a surgical abdomen or a clear obstruction right now. We’ll keep checking your exam closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned my bladder was huge on the x-ray. What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The x-ray noted a severely distended bladder, which can happen if you’re retaining urine. We’ll ask you about urination and check a bladder scan if needed—sometimes pain meds and dehydration can contribute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been peeing less because I haven’t been drinking. But I can go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. For now, we’re going to rest your gut—no tube feeds temporarily—give IV fluids, treat nausea, and control pain while we sort out the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop my feeds, won’t my sugar crash? That happened before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that closely. In the ER your fingerstick was 74, so they switched fluids to include dextrose. We’ll keep checking your blood sugars and adjust fluids so you don’t become hypoglycemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to get confused again like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. If you feel shaky, sweaty, lightheaded, or notice confusion, tell us right away. We’ll also keep your home meds that help your baseline GI issues, like rifaximin, unless there’s a reason to hold them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is a little better with the zofran, but the pain keeps coming back. What’s the plan for tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tonight we’ll continue IV fluids and bowel rest. We’ll trend labs, including lipase, and keep an eye on your abdominal exam. Given your history, we’re also planning more detailed imaging of the biliary tree and pancreas with an MRCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like an MRI? Do I have to drink contrast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s an MRI focused on the bile ducts and pancreas. In your case, they can give oral contrast through the gastrostomy tube. It helps us see anatomy without radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s an ulcer, how do you prove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The best test is an upper endoscopy—an EGD—where GI looks directly at the gastrojejunal connection and can treat an ulcer if they see one. We’re discussing that with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My diarrhea stopped. Does that mean it’s not C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It makes active C. diff less likely, especially since you’re not having ongoing watery stools here. If diarrhea returns, we can test, but right now it’s not the main concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or new diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No diarrhea. Still dry heaving sometimes. Pain is still there but maybe a little less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs remain stable, and your lipase has been coming down from where it started. That supports either a mild pancreatitis picture or a non-pancreatic cause with a transient lipase bump. We’re still going ahead with MRCP tonight to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could my antidepressant be causing pancreatitis? Someone mentioned that once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are rare reports of pancreatitis with fluoxetine. It’s uncommon, and we don’t have proof that’s what’s happening here, but it’s something we keep in mind while we evaluate other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to stop it suddenly. I get really anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not planning to stop it abruptly during this admission. We’ll focus on treating what’s in front of us and coordinate with your outpatient clinicians if medication changes ever become necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I restart my tube feeds? I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your pain and nausea are controlled and we’re confident there’s no acute obstruction or severe pancreatitis, we can restart feeds slowly. We’ll likely use your usual continuous NutriHep and monitor symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from MRCP. How are you feeling after the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. My stomach hurts from lying still. Did it show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Preliminary read is reassuring: the biliary tree and gallbladder look normal, and the pancreas looks normal without signs of acute inflammation. It also shows fast transit of contrast, which fits with your dumping syndrome history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It argues against significant acute pancreatitis or a biliary blockage. Given your symptoms and history, an ulcer at the anastomosis is moving higher on the list, and GI is planning an EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If they find an ulcer, can they fix it right then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often they can treat bleeding or high-risk spots during the procedure—like cauterizing a lesion—plus we treat with strong acid suppression and a coating medication to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. GI plans to do the EGD today. You’ll need to stay NPO—nothing by mouth—and we’ll keep tube feeds off until after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the scope. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable and typically don’t remember it. GI will review the risks and benefits with you beforehand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you worried about—bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking for a marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal connection, and if there’s a spot that looks like it could bleed, they can treat it. Your blood counts have been okay, and you haven’t reported black stools or vomiting blood, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from endoscopy. GI found a marginal ulcer with a pigmented lesion, and they cauterized it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was an ulcer. Is the cauterizing enough? Am I going to bleed later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Treating the lesion reduces the risk of bleeding. The bigger piece is healing the ulcer: we’re increasing acid suppression to pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and starting sucralfate four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I put the sucralfate through my tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI specifically wants it as a slurry by mouth, not through the tube, so it coats the area better. We’ll go over exactly how to take it before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not supposed to eat because of the hypoglycemia and confusion stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—your calories should still come from continuous tube feeds as you’ve been doing. The sucralfate is medication, not nutrition, and it’s a small volume. We’ll keep your feeding plan otherwise the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I restart NutriHep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can restart continuous tube feeds today at a low, steady rate and see how you tolerate it. We’ll keep it low protein as you’ve been doing given your chronic issues and prior episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds—can I stop the IV stuff? It makes me foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll transition from IV to oral pain medication as soon as you can tolerate it. The goal is to use the lowest effective dose and avoid constipation and sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with feeds back on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So far okay. No diarrhea. Pain is better, but still there when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep monitoring overnight. If things stay stable, we’ll plan discharge tomorrow with the new ulcer medications and a short course of oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement here. GI wanted some stool test, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’d like an H. pylori stool antigen test, but since you haven’t had a bowel movement in the hospital, we can’t send it now. We’ll make sure it’s on the plan to follow up in GI clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my hypoglycemia? Do I need endocrine again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your prior endocrine workup suggested a hyperinsulinemic state after gastric bypass, possibly from islet cell hyperplasia. During this admission, we focused on the ulcer, and your sugars have been stable with continuous feeds. We’ll keep your feeding strategy the same at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the confusion after meals—any new answers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new results came back during this stay. The prior workup didn’t show cirrhosis, and there’s still concern a urea cycle issue could contribute, especially with higher protein intake. That urea cycle panel from the prior admission is still pending, and you’ll review it with hepatology/GI outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep avoiding eating real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the plan you were discharged with previously—continuous tube feeds and avoid oral caloric intake unless your outpatient team changes it. For this ulcer, the key additions are pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I take the pantoprazole twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until you see GI. They want a repeat EGD in about 8 weeks to check healing, and you should stay on pantoprazole 40 mg every 12 hours until then unless GI advises otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the sucralfate—any timing with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can interfere with absorption of some medications. We’ll give you a schedule, but in general take it as directed four times daily and try to separate it from other meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home with pain meds. I get constipated fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing a short course of oxycodone for ulcer pain—about five days’ worth—and we’re also prescribing a bowel regimen: docusate twice daily and senna twice daily while you’re taking oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back like this, do I come straight to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe worsening pain, vomiting blood, black stools, fainting, fever, or you can’t keep feeds going, you should seek urgent care. For milder symptoms, call your GI team promptly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what exactly happened in the scope? The nurse said something about a pigmented spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw a marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with a pigmented lesion—an area that can indicate recent bleeding risk—and they cauterized it to reduce the chance of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my tube site—there’s always that granulation tissue and oozing. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw granulation tissue around the G-tube site, similar to before. We didn’t see signs of an acute infection. Keep your usual site care, and if you notice increasing redness, pus, fever, or worsening pain at the site, let your outpatient team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review the discharge plan: home today, continue continuous NutriHep tube feeds, start pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, take sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily, and follow up with GI in 8 weeks for repeat EGD. You’ll have oxycodone as needed for a few days plus stool softeners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds—rifaximin, ursodiol, fluoxetine, lorazepam, zolpidem, aripiprazole, atenolol—those stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your home regimen, and adding the ulcer medications. Use ondansetron as needed for nausea. If any medication causes new symptoms, call your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m relieved it wasn’t something surgical. I’ll set up the GI appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll send you with written instructions and the prescriptions. Please come back if you have any warning signs, and we’ll see you through GI follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube dependence, with history of dumping syndrome, post-bypass hypoglycemia, and recurrent marginal ulcers, was admitted for one week of nausea with dry heaving and diarrhea and one day of constant epigastric pain similar to prior ulcer episodes. Initial evaluation showed normal WBC and liver tests with mildly elevated lipase; she was managed conservatively with bowel rest, IV fluids (including dextrose for low fingerstick glucose), antiemetics, and analgesia while surgical causes were assessed and felt unlikely. Abdominal radiographs showed a nonspecific gas pattern and a distended bladder; MRCP demonstrated normal biliary tree and pancreas without acute inflammation. EGD revealed a marginal (gastrojejunal anastomotic) ulcer with a pigmented lesion that was cauterized; she was started on pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily, tube feeds were restarted and tolerated, and she was discharged home with short-course oxycodone and bowel regimen, with GI follow-up in 8 weeks for repeat EGD and outpatient H. pylori stool antigen testing when able.

conversation_lines.text: Your prior endocrine workup suggested a hyperinsulinemic state after gastric bypass, possibly from islet cell hyperplasia. During this admission, we focused on the ulcer, and your sugars have been stable with continuous feeds. We’ll keep your feeding strategy the same at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the confusion after meals—any new answers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new results came back during this stay. The prior workup didn’t show cirrhosis, and there’s still concern a urea cycle issue could contribute, especially with higher protein intake. That urea cycle panel from the prior admission is still pending, and you’ll review it with hepatology/GI outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep avoiding eating real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the plan you were discharged with previously—continuous tube feeds and avoid oral caloric intake unless your outpatient team changes it. For this ulcer, the key additions are pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I take the pantoprazole twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until you see GI. They want a repeat EGD in about 8 weeks to check healing, and you should stay on pantoprazole 40 mg every 12 hours until then unless GI advises otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the sucralfate—any timing with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can interfere with absorption of some medications. We’ll give you a schedule, but in general take it as directed four times daily and try to separate it from other meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home with pain meds. I get constipated fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing a short course of oxycodone for ulcer pain—about five days’ worth—and we’re also prescribing a bowel regimen: docusate twice daily and senna twice daily while you’re taking oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back like this, do I come straight to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe worsening pain, vomiting blood, black stools, fainting, fever, or you can’t keep feeds going, you should seek urgent care. For milder symptoms, call your GI team promptly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what exactly happened in the scope? The nurse said something about a pigmented spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw a marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with a pigmented lesion—an area that can indicate recent bleeding risk—and they cauterized it to reduce the chance of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my tube site—there’s always that granulation tissue and oozing. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw granulation tissue around the G-tube site, similar to before. We didn’t see signs of an acute infection. Keep your usual site care, and if you notice increasing redness, pus, fever, or worsening pain at the site, let your outpatient team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review the discharge plan: home today, continue continuous NutriHep tube feeds, start pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, take sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily, and follow up with GI in 8 weeks for repeat EGD. You’ll have oxycodone as needed for a few days plus stool softeners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds—rifaximin, ursodiol, fluoxetine, lorazepam, zolpidem, aripiprazole, atenolol—those stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your home regimen, and adding the ulcer medications. Use ondansetron as needed for nausea. If any medication causes new symptoms, call your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m relieved it wasn’t something surgical. I’ll set up the GI appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll send you with written instructions and the prescriptions. Please come back if you have any warning signs, and we’ll see you through GI follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube dependence, with history of dumping syndrome, post-bypass hypoglycemia, and recurrent marginal ulcers, was admitted for one week of nausea with dry heaving and diarrhea and one day of constant epigastric pain similar to prior ulcer episodes. Initial evaluation showed normal WBC and liver tests with mildly elevated lipase; she was managed conservatively with bowel rest, IV fluids (including dextrose for low fingerstick glucose), antiemetics, and analgesia while surgical causes were assessed and felt unlikely. Abdominal radiographs showed a nonspecific gas pattern and a distended bladder; MRCP demonstrated normal biliary tree and pancreas without acute inflammation. EGD revealed a marginal (gastrojejunal anastomotic) ulcer with a pigmented lesion that was cauterized; she was started on pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily, tube feeds were restarted and tolerated, and she was discharged home with short-course oxycodone and bowel regimen, with GI follow-up in 8 weeks for repeat EGD and outpatient H. pylori stool antigen testing when able.
